1.pericope_label: Lord, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me... Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the psalm through its close interweaving with the three psalms around it and takes the opening petitions as a prayer for the grace of silence, grounded in David's consciousness of sin against God; Ellicott works from the Hebrew, hearing the pillar of incense-smoke in the verb and insisting the lifted hands are a symbol of prayer rather than a term for oblation.

Gill reads the incense as prayer made fragrant through the mediation of Christ, suspects David feared speaking unadvisedly against the Lord's anointed, and is careful to deny that God ever inclines any man to sin; Calvin reports the En-gedi setting without committing to it and takes the psalm as a lesson in applying immediately to God.

Clarke argues from the Hebrew that no sacrifice is in view, the word being the unbloody meal offering, so that a man cut off from the sanctuary worships in spirit instead; Wesley extends the guard from wicked speech to every evil motion of the heart.

Henry takes the prayer as standing in place of the sacrifices David was banished from and reads the choice of the evening offering as pointing to Christ; Spurgeon hears a last resort, a cry feeble in itself but ennobled by its object.
Augustine refers the words to the whole Christ, spoken chiefly in the name of the Body, and takes the bloody sweat of the Head for the suffering of the martyrs throughout the Church.

positions.view: The persecution by Saul, perhaps the resolution to go to Achish of Gath.
Probably the cave of En-gedi, on the strength of the sixth verse, though not to be asserted.
The situation must be reconstructed from the psalm's links with its neighbours; the title alone does not settle it.

debates.question: Is the evening offering a sacrifice?

positions.view: Yes, and the prayer is offered in its place, the evening offering prefiguring Christ.
No; the word is the term for the unbloody meal offering, not for a slaughtered victim.
The offering is the flour and oil that followed the burnt offering, and the lifted hands are only a symbol of prayer.

outliers.note: Alone reads the psalm as the voice of the whole Christ, Head and Body, rather than of David in a particular distress.
Suspects the dainties are allurements rather than food, and connects the phrase with the casuistries by which laxer Jews excused joining heathen feasts.

themes: Lord, I cry unto thee: make haste unto me; give ear unto my voice, when I cry unto thee.
Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.
Incline not my heart to any evil thing, to practise wicked works with men that work iniquity: and let me not eat of their dainties.

5.pericope_label: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness... Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape

schools.summary: Delitzsch keeps the received accents and rejects the conditional rendering of the smiting, then notes how the psalm dies away in strains easy to understand; Ellicott lays out the textual alternatives at length, prefers the plough to the woodcutter in the seventh verse, reads the sixth ironically, and reports but rejects the easier variant 'their bones'.
Gill offers three constructions of the judges cast down by the rock, prophecy, release, or imprecation, and identifies the snare with the wife given to trap David or with the Ziphites.

Clarke follows the ancient versions in making the oil the wicked man's flattery, to be refused, canvasses several settings for the scattered bones without settling on one, and turns the last verse into a proverb about snares recoiling on those who set them; Wesley glosses the breaking as healing rather than hurting.

Henry takes the verse plainly, as a request to be told one's faults, the oil healing the bruise that sin itself made; Spurgeon keeps the received text and reads the scattered bones as the condition of the godly cause under Saul, without vitality, cohesion or headship.

debates.question: Whose oil is refused in the fifth verse?

positions.view: None is refused; the righteous man's reproof is itself the healing oil, and it will not break the head.
The oil is the wicked man's flattery, welcomed by no one who prefers a cutting reproof.
Both readings are defensible; the older versions support 'anoint' from a different text, which yields the better parallelism.
The received accents must stand, since the conditional rendering leaves the subject twice unexpressed.

debates.question: Whose scattered bones are at the grave's mouth?

positions.view: David's own party, the phrase being proverbial for men at the brink of ruin.
Possibly the priests massacred at Nob, in which case the phrase means at the command of Saul.
The godly cause itself, pictured as a skeleton broken and shovelled out of the grave.
The figure is the plough turning clods, not a woodcutter's yard, and the abrupt transition from the judges to the afflicted people should be preserved.

outliers.note: Concludes his survey of the sixth and seventh verses by admitting that he could contend for his own conjectures but that they are all too vague to ground an opinion.
Reads the sixth verse as irony, the ungodly hearing a dainty song of triumph rather than being entertained at a banquet.

themes: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil, which shall not break my head: for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities.
When their judges are overthrown in stony places, they shall hear my words; for they are sweet.
Our bones are scattered at the grave’s mouth, as when one cutteth and cleaveth wood upon the earth.
But mine eyes are unto thee, O God the Lord: in thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute.
Keep me from the snares which they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity.
Let the wicked fall into their own nets, whilst that I withal escape.
